passage: I was sitting on the wall outside tuition when Anjali started imitating the students of the school across the road: "They are all show-offs, they all cheat." Four of us laughed. Dilnaz, beside me, did not, and shifted her bag. Anjali's voice got louder with each laugh and the jokes got sharper. A girl from that school walked by and Anjali went quiet for a moment, then muttered one more joke. I cannot say what Anjali really thinks. Maybe the laughs feel good. But I noticed Dilnaz did not join in.

qa.q: What did Anjali say about the students of the school across the road?
qa.a: Anjali said, "They are all show-offs, they all cheat."

qa.q: Why might Anjali's jokes have gotten sharper with each laugh?
qa.a: Anjali may enjoy the group's approval, which rewards the joke and makes the label spread without being examined; the narrator cannot know for sure.

qa.q: What could someone do that keeps friendship but stops the label from spreading?
qa.a: Someone could say "all of them? I know one who is nice", or steer the talk elsewhere, without a lecture, so the joke does not get more laughs.

qa.q: What might Dilnaz be feeling by not laughing and shifting the bag?
qa.a: Dilnaz may feel uncomfortable with the sweeping label but reluctant to speak against the group, which the shifting bag hints at.

grounding: A teenager describes people from another school with sweeping labels, and the group's approval rewards the joke so the label spreads unexamined.

passage: Monday. On the school bus Zubin said the kids from the colony behind the market "never study and always fight." Everyone laughed, and Jatin, next to him, said nothing. Wednesday. Zubin repeated it in the canteen, and a new boy laughed too, eager to be liked. Zubin felt taller. Saturday. At a cricket match Zubin met Rohan from that colony and was stunned: Rohan was polite, an excellent bowler, and ended up lending Zubin a spare pair of gloves. That night Zubin looked at Jatin and, for once, did not make a joke.

qa.q: What did Zubin say about the colony behind the market?
qa.a: Zubin said the kids from the colony behind the market "never study and always fight."

qa.q: Why did Zubin feel taller after the canteen laugh?
qa.a: The group's approval rewarded the joke, so Zubin felt bigger and safer inside the group; the label felt like belonging.

qa.q: What turning point on Saturday changed Zubin's thinking?
qa.a: Meeting Rohan, a polite and excellent bowler who lent spare gloves, showed Zubin a real person that did not match the label.

qa.q: What might Jatin have been thinking when saying nothing on the bus?
qa.a: Jatin may have disliked the sweeping remark but did not want to break from the laughing group, so kept quiet.

grounding: A teenager describes people from another neighbourhood with sweeping labels, the group approves, and meeting an individual shakes the label.

passage:
Okay, you asked about the river colony kids. I'm Harsha, and I'll be honest about how we talked.
In our group, the joke was that everyone from across the river was a thief. If someone lost a pen, we'd say, “Check the river colony boys.” Everyone laughed. The more you said it, the more people liked you.
I never met anyone from there. I didn't need to. The joke did the work.
Then, at the district cricket camp, I was paired with Amandeep. Turned out he was from river colony. He lent me his gloves on the first day.
I didn't tell my friends. I still laughed at the joke once or twice. It makes me sad now, how easily it came out of my mouth.

qa.q: Who lent Harsha gloves on the first day?
qa.a: Amandeep lent Harsha his gloves.

qa.q: How does Harsha feel now about the joke?
qa.a: Harsha feels sad and a bit ashamed at how easily the label came out, even after meeting Amandeep.

qa.q: What could Harsha do next time the joke comes up?
qa.a: Harsha could say something simple like, "One of them lent me gloves, actually," which questions the label without a fight.

qa.q: How might Amandeep feel if he heard the joke?
qa.a: He would likely feel hurt and angry at being called a thief just for where he lives.

grounding: A teenager admits using a sweeping label about kids from another colony because the group rewarded the joke, without examining it.

passage:
Monday: After the inter-school debate, Lakshmi's friends in the bus laughed about the students from the international school. “Rich brats. They buy their marks,” said Pooja. Lakshmi added, “And their parents write their speeches.” Everyone roared.
Wednesday: In the class group chat, Lakshmi posted a meme about “international school kids” who can't tie their shoes. Twenty laughing reactions. She felt great.
The next Monday: Siddharth, the debater from that school, who had beaten them, posted his thank-you note online. He wrote about practising in his aunt's bookshop after closing. Lakshmi read it twice. Nobody in her group mentioned it. The meme was already being shared by the juniors.

qa.q: How many laughing reactions did the meme get?
qa.a: It got twenty laughing reactions.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel when she posted the meme?
qa.a: She felt great, enjoying the approval of her friends.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could Lakshmi do now?
qa.a: The label spread because it got laughs and nobody checked it; Lakshmi could share Siddharth's note in the chat or stop reposting the meme.

qa.q: How might Siddharth feel if he saw the meme?
qa.a: He would likely feel hurt and unfairly judged, since he practised hard in his aunt's bookshop.

grounding: Shows a teenager joining in sweeping labels about another school because the group rewards the joke, so the label spreads unexamined.

passage:
Pranav, you're laughing about the kids from the other school. Let me tell you something. I'm your Vandana bua, and at your age I was worse.
In our town there was the railway colony, near the tracks. My friends and I called all those kids “rowdies”. If anything got broken, it was the railway kids. If a boy whistled, it was the railway kids. We said it and laughed, and each time the laugh made us closer.
I never actually knew one of them.
Years later, at college, my closest friend, Shobha, told me she grew up in that colony. She had heard us, she said, all those years ago, walking past our gate.
I still feel a heaviness in my chest when I think of it.

qa.q: What did young Vandana and her friends call the railway colony kids?
qa.a: They called them "rowdies".

qa.q: How does Vandana feel remembering it now?
qa.a: She feels sad and ashamed, with a heaviness in her chest.

qa.q: At what point in the story could young Vandana have made a different choice?
qa.a: Any time the group laughed, she could have asked if they actually knew any railway kids, instead of repeating the label.

qa.q: How might Shobha have felt as a child walking past their gate?
qa.a: She probably felt hurt and small, hearing girls label all the children of her colony as rowdies.

grounding: An elder recalls how as a teen she used a sweeping label for another colony's kids because the group's laughter rewarded it.

passage:
The school bus coughed and died on the flyover, forty minutes from home, in the June heat. The driver phoned for help: the Sector 9 school's bus would pick them up on its route.
"Great," Thomas announced. "Now we ride with the Sector 9 lot. Hold your bags, that lot all steal." The back rows laughed. Saurabh added, "And they can't even speak properly." More laughter. Thomas felt the warm buzz of it, everyone looking at him.
When the other bus arrived, the kids inside shuffled over without a word to make room. A boy in a faded blue uniform lifted Saurabh's cricket kit onto the rack for him. Nobody said thank you.
By evening, "Sector 9 steals" was a running joke in the class chat. Thomas had never been to Sector 9. He didn't know a single person from there. He hadn't thought about that.

qa.q: Where did the school bus break down?
qa.a: On the flyover, forty minutes from home.

qa.q: Why did Thomas keep joking about the Sector 9 kids?
qa.a: Thomas enjoyed the warm buzz of the group laughing and looking at him; the approval felt so good that he never questioned the label.

qa.q: What could Thomas ask himself before a joke like that next time?
qa.a: Whether he actually knows anyone from the group, and whether he would say it to the boy who lifted Saurabh's kit.

qa.q: What was it like for the Sector 9 kids to make room for the stranded students?
qa.a: They helped quietly, even lifting a kit, yet got no thanks and were being called thieves behind their backs.

grounding: Shows a teenager labelling kids from another school with sweeping stereotypes, rewarded by group laughter so the label spreads unexamined.
